modern-spread-rest-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** does mutating the source array after spreading affect the spread result? **The answer: no — `b` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.** **Why:** spread performs a **shallow copy** at the moment the expression evaluates, reading the elements of `a` then and there into a brand-new array. **Why later `a.push(99)` doesn't matter:** `b` is independent — spread creates no live link to `a`. **The shallow caveat:** only the top level is copied; nested objects/arrays would still be shared by reference. **Common mistakes:** expecting spread to be a live view of the source, or assuming it deep-copies nested structures (it doesn't — use `structuredClone` for that).
modern-spread-rest-mcq-003.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3];
const b = [...a, 4, 5]; // snapshot copy of a's current elements
a.push(99);             // mutates a, not b
console.log(b); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
console.log(a); // [1, 2, 3, 99]
```

modern-optional-nullish-001.explanation: **The problem:** reading a deeply nested property throws if an intermediate value is `null`/`undefined`. **What `?.` does:** optional chaining **short-circuits** — if the value immediately to its left is `null` or `undefined`, the whole expression stops and evaluates to `undefined` instead of throwing a `TypeError`. **Why it works:** `?.` checks for nullish before accessing the next link, so `a?.b?.c` safely yields `undefined` the moment any link is nullish. **It also guards calls/indexes:** `obj.method?.()`, `arr?.[i]`. **Common mistakes:** thinking `?.` suppresses *all* errors (it only guards nullish access — a non-nullish but wrong type still throws), or overusing it where a value is guaranteed to exist (hides real bugs).
modern-optional-nullish-001.example:
```js
const user = { profile: { name: 'Ada' } };
console.log(user?.profile?.name);    // 'Ada'
console.log(user?.address?.city);    // undefined — no throw
console.log(user?.greet?.());        // undefined — optional call
const arr = null;
console.log(arr?.[0]);               // undefined — optional index
```

modern-optional-nullish-002.explanation: **The problem:** `||` and `??` both supply defaults but disagree on `0`, `''`, and `false`. **`??` (nullish coalescing):** falls back **only** when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. **`||` (logical OR):** falls back for **any falsy** value — `0`, `''`, `false`, `NaN`, `null`, `undefined`. **Why the difference matters:** `0` and `''` are often **legitimate** values; `||` would wrongly replace them with the default, while `??` preserves them. **The rule of thumb:** use `??` when only "missing" (`null`/`undefined`) should trigger the default; use `||` when any falsy value should. **Common mistakes:** using `||` for numeric/string defaults and silently clobbering valid `0`/`''`.
modern-optional-nullish-002.example:
```js
console.log(0 ?? 'default');  // 0        — 0 is not nullish
console.log(0 || 'default');  // 'default' — 0 is falsy
console.log('' ?? 'default'); // ''       — '' is not nullish
console.log('' || 'default'); // 'default' — '' is falsy
console.log(null ?? 'default'); // 'default' — null is nullish
```

modern-optional-nullish-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** chaining `?.` past a `null` value and past a missing key — both print `undefined`. **Why `obj?.a?.b?.c` is `undefined`:** `obj.a.b` is `null`; the next `?.c` sees a nullish left side and **short-circuits to `undefined`** (not a `TypeError`, and not `null`). **Why `obj?.x?.y` is `undefined`:** `obj.x` is missing → `undefined`, so `?.y` short-circuits. **The key detail:** optional chaining always yields **`undefined`** when it short-circuits, regardless of whether the nullish value was `null` or `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** expecting a `TypeError` for `null?.c` (it's guarded), or expecting the result to be `null` when the nullish link was `null` (it's normalized to `undefined`).
modern-optional-nullish-mcq-003.example:
```js
const obj = { a: { b: null } };
console.log(obj?.a?.b?.c); // undefined — null?.c short-circuits (no throw)
console.log(obj?.x?.y);    // undefined — obj.x is missing
console.log(obj?.a?.b);    // null      — last link is the actual value
```

modern-esm-001.explanation: **The problem:** ES Modules offer two export styles with different import syntax. **Named exports:** `export const foo = …` — imported by **exact name** with braces: `import { foo } from './mod.js'` (rename with `as`). A module can have **many**. **Default export:** `export default value` — imported with **any name, no braces**: `import whatever from './mod.js'`. A module has **at most one**. **Why both exist:** named exports are explicit, searchable, and tree-shakeable; a default suits a module's single primary value. **You can mix** one default with several named. **Common mistakes:** using braces for a default import (or omitting them for a named one), or expecting two default exports in a file.

modern-esm-002.explanation: **The problem:** you want all of a module's named exports grouped under one object instead of importing each. **The syntax:** `import * as name from './mod.js'` creates a **namespace object** whose properties are the module's named exports (a `default` export appears as `name.default`). **Why it's useful:** it namespaces related utilities (`math.add`, `math.sub`) and documents where each came from. **A detail:** the namespace object is **read-only** and **live** — its bindings reflect the module's current values, but you can't reassign them. **Common mistakes:** trying to mutate the namespace (`math.add = …` throws in strict mode), or expecting the default export under its own name rather than `.default`.

modern-esm-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** the key difference between ES Modules and CommonJS `require`. **The answer:** ESM `import`/`export` are **static** — declarations are resolved at **parse time**, before any code runs, building the dependency graph up front. CommonJS `require()` is a **runtime function call**, evaluated when reached, so it can sit inside `if`/loops. **Why static matters:** it enables **tree-shaking** (dead-export elimination), better circular-dependency handling, and live bindings. **Why the other options are wrong:** ESM isn't "async vs sync" in that simplistic sense, CommonJS *does* support named-ish exports via `module.exports`, and Node has supported ESM for years (`.mjs` or `"type": "module"`). **Common mistakes:** putting `import` inside a block (illegal — use dynamic `import()` for conditional loading).

array-at-001.explanation: **The problem:** reading from the end of an array historically needed `arr[arr.length - 1]`, which is verbose and error-prone. **What `at()` does:** it takes an integer index and returns that element, but **negative indices count from the end** — `at(-1)` is the last element, `at(-2)` the second-to-last. **Why it works:** `at()` adds `length` to a negative index before lookup, so `-1` maps to `length - 1`. **Why it's nicer:** no repeated `arr.length` and it reads clearly. **Common mistakes:** thinking bracket notation supports negatives (`arr[-1]` is just a string property `'-1'`, always `undefined`), or that `at()` mutates anything (it's a pure read).
array-at-001.example:
```js
const a = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
console.log(a.at(-1)); // 'c' — last element
console.log(a.at(0));  // 'a'
console.log(a[-1]);    // undefined — bracket notation has no negative indexing
```

array-at-002.explanation: **The problem:** what does `at()` return for an out-of-range index? **The answer: `undefined`** — just like bracket access, an index past the end yields `undefined`, not an error. **Why:** `at()` is a plain element read; there's no bounds checking that throws. The only thing that throws on arrays is an invalid *length* (e.g. `new Array(-1)`), not an out-of-range read. **Why it matters:** you can safely probe indices without `try/catch`. **Common mistakes:** expecting a `RangeError` for `a.at(5)` on a 3-element array, or confusing `at()` with typed-array/`String` behavior (both also return `undefined` for OOB).
array-at-002.example:
```js
const a = [10, 20, 30];
console.log(a.at(5));  // undefined — out of range, no error
console.log(a.at(2));  // 30
console.log(a.at(-5)); // undefined — too far negative
```

array-concat-001.explanation: **The problem:** does `concat()` change the arrays it joins? **The answer: no** — `concat()` is **non-mutating**; it returns a **brand-new array** containing the elements of the original plus the arguments, leaving all inputs untouched. **Why it works:** `concat` reads through its inputs and copies element references into a fresh array (a shallow copy). **Why it matters:** it's safe in immutable/functional code, unlike `push`/`splice`. **Common mistakes:** assuming it mutates like `push`, or expecting a **deep** copy — nested objects are shared by reference between the source and the result.

array-concat-002.explanation: **The problem:** how deep does `concat()` flatten its array arguments? **The answer: one level only.** `concat` spreads the **top-level** elements of each array argument into the result; it does **not** recurse into nested arrays. So `[[1]].concat([2, [3]])` keeps `[1]` and `[3]` as nested arrays, giving `[[1], 2, [3]]`. **Why:** `concat` treats each argument that is an array by appending its elements, but those elements (including inner arrays) are copied as-is. **Common mistakes:** expecting full flattening (use `flat()`/`flatMap()` for that), or thinking non-array arguments are spread (a non-array is appended whole).
array-concat-002.example:
```js
const a = [[1]];
const b = [2, [3]];
console.log(a.concat(b)); // [[1], 2, [3]] — only one level merged
console.log([1].concat(2, [3, 4])); // [1, 2, 3, 4] — array args spread once
console.log([1].concat([[2]]));     // [1, [2]] — inner array kept nested
```

array-copyWithin-001.explanation: **The problem:** `copyWithin(target, start)` copies a slice of the array onto another position **within the same array**, in place. **How it works:** it copies elements from `start` (to the end, here) and pastes them beginning at `target`, **overwriting** without changing the array's length. So `[1,2,3,4,5].copyWithin(0, 3)` copies `[4,5]` (from index 3) over indices 0–1 → `[4,5,3,4,5]`. **Why it mutates:** it's an in-place shift-style operation (originally for typed arrays/performance). **Common mistakes:** expecting a new array (it returns the *same*, mutated array), or forgetting the length is fixed — copying never grows or shrinks the array.
array-copyWithin-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const r = a.copyWithin(0, 3); // copy from index 3 onward to index 0
console.log(r);        // [4, 5, 3, 4, 5]
console.log(a === r);  // true — same array, mutated in place
```

array-copyWithin-002.explanation: **The problem:** with the third argument, `copyWithin(target, start, end)` copies only the slice `[start, end)`. **The walk-through:** `[1,2,3,4,5].copyWithin(0, 3, 4)` copies elements from index 3 up to (not including) 4 — that's just `[4]` — and pastes it at index 0, giving `[4,2,3,4,5]`. **Why only one element changes:** `end` is **exclusive**, so `start=3, end=4` selects a single element. **Why the rest is unchanged:** only the copied range overwrites; everything else stays. **Common mistakes:** treating `end` as inclusive, or expecting the whole tail to be copied when an `end` limits it.
array-copyWithin-002.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
a.copyWithin(0, 3, 4); // copy [index 3, index 4) = [4] to index 0
console.log(a); // [4, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

array-entries-001.explanation: **The problem:** you often need both the index and the value while iterating. **What `entries()` returns:** an **array iterator** that yields a two-element array `[index, value]` for each position. **Why it's useful:** combined with `for...of` and destructuring (`for (const [i, v] of arr.entries())`) it gives clean index+value iteration without a manual counter. **A detail:** it's lazy (an iterator), and it visits holes in sparse arrays as `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** expecting a plain array of pairs (it's an iterator — spread it with `[...arr.entries()]` to materialize), or confusing it with `Object.entries` (which returns string keys).
array-entries-001.example:
```js
const a = ['x', 'y', 'z'];
for (const [i, v] of a.entries()) console.log(i, v); // 0 x | 1 y | 2 z
console.log([...a.entries()]); // [[0,'x'],[1,'y'],[2,'z']]
```

array-entries-002.explanation: **The problem:** how does `entries()` treat empty slots (holes) in a sparse array? **The answer:** it **visits every index**, yielding holes as `undefined`. So `[, 'a']` (a hole at 0, `'a'` at 1) iterates **twice**: `[0, undefined]` then `[1, 'a']`. **Why:** the iterator-producing methods (`entries`, `keys`, `values`) are **not** hole-skipping — unlike `forEach`/`map`/`filter`, which skip holes. **Why this distinction matters:** sparse arrays behave inconsistently across methods, a frequent source of bugs. **Common mistakes:** assuming `entries()` skips holes like `forEach`, or that a leading comma `[, 'a']` creates `undefined` at index 0 (it's a true hole, reported as `undefined` here).
array-entries-002.example:
```js
const sparse = [, 'a']; // hole at index 0
console.log([...sparse.entries()]); // [[0, undefined], [1, 'a']] — visits the hole
console.log(sparse.length);         // 2
// contrast: forEach skips the hole entirely
sparse.forEach((v, i) => console.log('forEach', i, v)); // only: forEach 1 a
```

array-every-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `every()` return for an **empty** array? **The answer: `true`** — vacuously, since there's no element that fails the test. **Why:** `every()` returns `true` unless it finds an element for which the callback is falsy; with zero elements, it never finds one. This mirrors the logician's "all of an empty set" being true. **Why it matters:** guard logic like `items.every(valid)` passes for empty inputs — sometimes desired, sometimes a bug. **Common mistakes:** expecting `false` for `[]`, or forgetting the symmetric quirk that `[].some(...)` returns `false`.
array-every-001.example:
```js
console.log([].every((x) => x > 0));       // true  — vacuously true
console.log([2, 4, 6].every((x) => x % 2 === 0)); // true
console.log([2, 3, 4].every((x) => x % 2 === 0)); // false — 3 fails
console.log([].some((x) => x > 0));        // false — the symmetric case
```

array-every-002.explanation: **The problem:** how does `every()` behave once an element fails the predicate? **The answer:** it **short-circuits** — the moment the callback returns falsy, `every()` stops iterating and returns `false`, skipping all remaining elements. **Why:** as soon as one element fails, the "all pass" result is decided, so continuing would be wasted work. **Why it matters:** side effects in the callback won't run for elements after the first failure, and it's efficient on large arrays. **Common mistakes:** expecting `every()` to visit all elements (it doesn't past the first failure), or relying on it to collect *all* failures (it returns a single boolean).

array-fill-001.explanation: **The problem:** `fill(value, start, end)` overwrites a range of an array with a static value, in place. **The walk-through:** `[1,2,3].fill(0, 1, 2)` fills index 1 up to (not including) 2 with `0` → `[1,0,3]`. **Why:** `start` is inclusive, `end` exclusive; omitting them fills the whole array. **Why it mutates:** `fill` writes into the existing array and returns it (handy for initializing, e.g. `Array(n).fill(0)`). **Common mistakes:** treating `end` as inclusive, or using `fill({})`/`fill([])` and not realizing **the same reference** is placed in every slot (see the next card).
array-fill-001.example:
```js
console.log([1, 2, 3].fill(0, 1, 2)); // [1, 0, 3] — index 1 only
console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].fill(9));    // [9, 9, 9, 9] — whole array
console.log(Array(3).fill(0));        // [0, 0, 0] — common init idiom
```

array-fill-002.explanation: **The problem:** `Array(3).fill({})` then mutating `arr[0]` changes `arr[1]` too — `arr[1].x` is `42`. **Why it happens:** `fill` places the **same value** in every slot. With an object literal, that value is **one reference**, so all three slots point at the **same object**; mutating it through any index is visible through all. **Why it's a classic bug:** people expect `fill({})` to create independent objects (it doesn't). **The fix:** build distinct objects with `Array.from({length: 3}, () => ({}))`. **Common mistakes:** the same trap with `fill([])` for grids, and assuming `fill` evaluates the argument per slot (it's evaluated once).

array-filter-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `filter()` return when nothing passes the test? **The answer: an empty array `[]`** — never `undefined` or `null`. **Why:** `filter()` always returns a **new array** of the elements for which the callback was truthy; if none qualify, that array is simply empty. **Why it matters:** the result is always safely chainable/iterable (`.length`, `.map`, etc.) without null checks. **Common mistakes:** expecting `undefined` for no matches (that's `find()`), or `-1` (that's `findIndex`); and forgetting `filter` always allocates a fresh array even when empty.
array-filter-001.example:
```js
const r = [1, 2, 3].filter((n) => n > 10);
console.log(r);         // [] — empty, not undefined
console.log(r.length);  // 0
console.log(Array.isArray(r)); // true — always an array
```

array-filter-002.explanation: **The problem:** how does `filter()` treat empty slots in a sparse array? **The answer:** it **skips holes** — the callback is never invoked for an empty slot — and the **returned array is dense** (holes are dropped, not preserved as `undefined`). **Why:** `filter` is one of the hole-skipping iteration methods (with `forEach`, `map`, `some`, `every`), and since holes never pass an un-run test, they simply don't appear in the output. **Why it matters:** `filter(Boolean)` is a common way to compact arrays and remove falsy values and holes at once. **Common mistakes:** expecting holes to surface as `undefined` in the result, or that the callback runs for every index.
array-filter-002.example:
```js
const sparse = [1, , 3]; // hole at index 1
const r = sparse.filter(() => true); // callback skips the hole
console.log(r);        // [1, 3] — dense, hole removed
console.log(r.length); // 2
```

array-filter-003.explanation: **The problem:** `filter((n, i) => i % 2 === 0)` keeps elements at **even indices**, giving `[1, 3]`, not `[2, 4]`. **Why:** the callback's second parameter is the **index**, and the predicate tests the index, not the value. Indices `0` and `2` satisfy `i % 2 === 0`, whose values are `1` and `3`. **Why people slip:** they read `i % 2 === 0` as "even values" and forget the parameter is the position. **Why it matters:** index-based filtering (every other element, pagination) is common. **Common mistakes:** confusing the value and index parameters, or assuming `0`-based indices start at `1`.
array-filter-003.example:
```js
const r = [1, 2, 3, 4].filter((n, i) => i % 2 === 0); // keep even INDICES
console.log(r); // [1, 3] — values at indices 0 and 2
// value-based instead:
console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].filter((n) => n % 2 === 0)); // [2, 4]
```

array-find-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `find()` return when no element matches? **The answer: `undefined`.** `find()` returns the **first element** for which the callback is truthy, or `undefined` if none qualify. **Why:** it's designed to retrieve a value, so "not found" is the absence-of-value sentinel `undefined`. **Contrast:** `findIndex()` returns `-1` for no match (it deals in positions). **Why it matters:** always handle the `undefined` case before using the result (`?.` or a guard). **Common mistakes:** expecting `null` or `-1`, or treating a falsy *found* value (like `0` or `''`) as "not found" — check existence carefully.

array-find-002.explanation: **The problem:** does `find()` skip holes like `forEach`/`filter`? **The answer: no** — `find()` (and `findIndex`/`findLast`/`findLastIndex`) **visit every index**, treating empty slots as `undefined`. **Why:** these methods must inspect each position to decide a match, so they don't take the hole-skipping shortcut. **Why it matters:** a predicate like `(x) => x === undefined` can "match" a hole, which surprises people who assume holes are invisible. **Common mistakes:** assuming all array iterators behave the same about holes — the `find` family does not skip them, unlike `forEach`/`map`/`filter`/`some`/`every`.

array-find-003.explanation: **The problem:** `find()` and `findIndex()` differ in their "not found" sentinel. **The answer:** when nothing matches, **`find()` returns `undefined`** (it yields the element/value) and **`findIndex()` returns `-1`** (it yields a position). **Why two sentinels:** `undefined` is the natural "no value", and `-1` is the conventional "no index" (matching `indexOf`). **Why it matters:** you must test the right sentinel — `if (idx !== -1)` for `findIndex`, `if (found !== undefined)` (or `?.`) for `find`. **Common mistakes:** checking `find()`'s result against `-1`, or `findIndex()`'s against `undefined` — both silently misbehave.
array-find-003.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(a.find((n) => n > 5));      // undefined
console.log(a.findIndex((n) => n > 5)); // -1
console.log(a.find((n) => n === 2));    // 2
console.log(a.findIndex((n) => n === 2));// 1
```

array-findIndex-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `findIndex()` return when no element satisfies the callback? **The answer: `-1`.** `findIndex()` returns the **index** of the first matching element, or `-1` when none match — mirroring `indexOf`'s convention. **Why `-1`:** it's an impossible real index, so it unambiguously signals "not found" while staying a number. **Why it matters:** guard with `if (i !== -1)` before using the index; using `-1` as an index (`arr[-1]`) is `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** expecting `undefined` (that's `find()`), or treating `0` (a valid found index) as falsy/not-found in an `if (i)` check.
array-findIndex-001.example:
```js
const a = [5, 12, 8, 130];
console.log(a.findIndex((n) => n > 100)); // 3
console.log(a.findIndex((n) => n > 999)); // -1 — none match
const i = a.findIndex((n) => n === 5);
console.log(i, i !== -1 ? a[i] : 'none'); // 0 5 — note: use !== -1, not truthiness
```

array-findIndex-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[5, 12, 8, 130].findIndex(n => n > 10)` returns `1`, not `12` or `0`. **Why:** `findIndex()` returns the **index** of the **first** element passing the test. The first element greater than 10 is `12`, which sits at **index 1** — so the result is `1`. **Why not `12`:** that's the value; `findIndex` returns the position (use `find` for the value). **Why not `0`:** `5` (index 0) fails the test. **Why it short-circuits:** it stops at the first match. **Common mistakes:** confusing the returned index with the matching value, or expecting it to scan past the first hit.
array-findIndex-002.example:
```js
const a = [5, 12, 8, 130];
console.log(a.findIndex((n) => n > 10)); // 1 — index of 12 (first match)
console.log(a.find((n) => n > 10));      // 12 — the value, for contrast
```

array-findLast-001.explanation: **The problem:** `find()` searches front-to-back; how do you get the **last** match? **`findLast()`** iterates **right-to-left** and returns the first match from the end. For `[4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12]` with `n % 2 !== 0` (odd), scanning from the end finds `11` before `7`/`5`, so it returns `11`. **Why it exists (ES2023):** previously you'd `reverse()` (mutates/copies) or compute an index manually; `findLast` does it directly and lazily. **Why it returns `undefined` for no match:** same value-sentinel as `find`. **Common mistakes:** assuming it returns the *largest* matching value (it returns the *last by position*), or that it mutates (it doesn't).
array-findLast-001.example:
```js
const a = [4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12];
console.log(a.findLast((n) => n % 2 !== 0)); // 11 — last odd by position
console.log(a.find((n) => n % 2 !== 0));     // 5  — first odd, for contrast
```

array-findLast-002.explanation: **The problem:** which ES version added `findLast()` / `findLastIndex()`? **The answer: ES2023.** They shipped alongside the other ES2023 array additions — the immutable `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, and `with`. **Why know this:** these are recent, so very old runtimes lack them (modern Node and evergreen browsers have them). **Why they were added:** to search from the end without reversing the array. **Common mistakes:** confusing them with `find`/`findIndex` (ES2015) or assuming they're as universally available as the older methods; in legacy environments you'd polyfill or reverse-and-`find`.
array-findLast-002.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
// ES2023 family:
console.log(a.findLast((n) => n < 4));      // 3
console.log(a.findLastIndex((n) => n < 4)); // 2
console.log(typeof Array.prototype.findLast); // 'function' in modern runtimes
```

array-findLastIndex-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `findLastIndex()` return with no match? **The answer: `-1`** — the same "no index" sentinel as `findIndex`/`indexOf`. **What it does:** scans **right-to-left** and returns the **index** of the first element (from the end) that passes the test, or `-1` if none do. **Why `-1`:** consistency with the index-returning family. **Why it matters:** guard with `!== -1` before indexing. **Common mistakes:** expecting `undefined` (that's `findLast`), or assuming the returned index is relative to a reversed array — it's the element's **real** index in the original array.
array-findLastIndex-001.example:
```js
const a = [4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12];
console.log(a.findLastIndex((n) => n % 2 !== 0)); // 5 — index of 11
console.log(a.findLastIndex((n) => n > 100));     // -1 — none match
```

array-findLastIndex-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[4,5,7,8,9,11,12].findLastIndex(n => n % 2 !== 0)` returns `5`. **The walk-through:** scanning from the end, the elements are `12`(6, even), `11`(5, odd ✓) — so the first odd from the right is `11` at **index 5**. **Why not `6`:** index 6 holds `12`, which is even. **Why not `11`:** that's the value, not the index — `findLastIndex` returns the position. **Why not `2`:** index 2 (`7`) is odd but it's the match `findIndex` would return going forward, not the last one. **Common mistakes:** confusing value with index, or scanning left-to-right.
array-findLastIndex-002.example:
```js
const a = [4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12];
console.log(a.findLastIndex((n) => n % 2 !== 0)); // 5 — index of 11 (last odd)
console.log(a[5]); // 11
```

array-flat-001.explanation: **The problem:** what's the default flattening depth of `flat()`? **The answer: `1`** — called with no argument, `flat()` removes a **single** level of nesting. **Why a default of 1:** the most common case is un-nesting one layer; deeper flattening is opt-in. **How to go deeper:** pass a number (`flat(2)`) or `Infinity` for any depth. **A bonus:** `flat()` also **removes holes** while flattening. **Common mistakes:** expecting `flat()` to fully flatten nested arrays (it stops at one level), or passing a boolean/expecting recursion by default.

array-flat-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, 2, , 4].flat()` returns `[1, 2, 4]` — the hole vanishes. **Why:** besides flattening one level, `flat()` **drops empty slots** (holes) from the result, producing a dense array. So the hole between `2` and `4` is removed rather than becoming `undefined`. **Why it's handy:** `arr.flat()` is a quick way to compact a sparse array (even with no nesting to flatten). **Why not `[1,2,undefined,4]`:** holes are not the same as `undefined` values — `flat` discards holes but would *keep* an explicit `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** confusing holes with `undefined`, or expecting `flat()` to preserve sparseness.
array-flat-002.example:
```js
console.log([1, 2, , 4].flat());          // [1, 2, 4] — hole removed
console.log([1, 2, undefined, 4].flat()); // [1, 2, undefined, 4] — value kept
console.log([1, 2, , 4].length);          // 4 (sparse) before flat
```

array-flat-003.explanation: **The problem:** how do you fully flatten an array nested to an unknown/arbitrary depth? **The answer: `arr.flat(Infinity)`.** Passing `Infinity` as the depth tells `flat()` to recurse through **every** level, returning a single flat array. **Why `Infinity` works:** the depth argument is compared each level; `Infinity` never runs out, so flattening continues until no nested arrays remain. **Why not a huge number:** `Infinity` is clearer and guaranteed sufficient. **Common mistakes:** using `flat()` (depth 1) and expecting full flattening, or hand-writing recursion when one `flat(Infinity)` call suffices.

array-flatMap-001.explanation: **The problem:** mapping then flattening is a common two-step (`arr.map(fn).flat()`). **What `flatMap()` does:** it runs the callback over each element and **flattens the result by one level** in a **single pass** — equivalent to `map(fn).flat()` but more efficient (no intermediate array) and clearer in intent. **The key limit:** it flattens **exactly one** level, no more. **Why it's useful:** expanding each element into zero, one, or many outputs (tokenizing, one-to-many). **Common mistakes:** expecting deep flattening (it's one level — use `map().flat(Infinity)` for more), or returning a deeply nested array and being surprised it isn't fully flattened.

array-flatMap-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1,2,3].flatMap(x => [[x*2]])` yields `[[2],[4],[6]]`, not `[2,4,6]`. **Why:** `flatMap` flattens **only one level**. The callback returns `[[2]]` (an array containing an array); flattening once removes the **outer** wrapper, leaving `[2]` per element → `[[2],[4],[6]]`. **Why not `[2,4,6]`:** that would require flattening two levels. **Why not `[[2,4,6]]`:** each element maps independently, then results concatenate. **Common mistakes:** assuming `flatMap` fully flattens, or miscounting the nesting the callback returns.
array-flatMap-002.example:
```js
console.log([1, 2, 3].flatMap((x) => [[x * 2]])); // [[2], [4], [6]] — one level off
console.log([1, 2, 3].flatMap((x) => [x * 2]));   // [2, 4, 6]       — single-wrapped
```

array-flatMap-003.explanation: **The problem:** how do you transform *and* filter in one pass with `flatMap()`? **The technique:** return an **empty array `[]`** from the callback for elements to **drop**, and a **single-element array `[value]`** for elements to **keep** (optionally transformed). Because `flatMap` flattens one level, the `[]`s contribute nothing and the `[value]`s unwrap into the result. **Why it's useful:** it's a combined map+filter that avoids two passes, and can also expand one element into many. **Common mistakes:** returning a bare value instead of an array when you also want to sometimes drop (mixing shapes), or returning `null`/`undefined` to drop (those become elements, not removals).

array-forEach-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `forEach()` return? **The answer: always `undefined`.** `forEach` is for **side effects** — it runs the callback for each element and returns nothing useful. **Why:** it deliberately has no result so you don't chain off it; for transformations use `map`, for accumulation use `reduce`. **Why it matters:** `const x = arr.forEach(...)` always makes `x` undefined — a common confusion. **Common mistakes:** expecting `forEach` to return a new/filtered array (use `map`/`filter`), or trying to chain `.forEach(...).map(...)` (the second call would be on `undefined`).
array-forEach-001.example:
```js
const r = [1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => n * 2);
console.log(r); // undefined — forEach returns nothing

let sum = 0;
[1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => { sum += n; }); // side effect
console.log(sum); // 6
```

array-forEach-002.explanation: **The problem:** `forEach` with an `async` callback doesn't wait for the awaited work. **Why it happens:** `forEach` **ignores the return value** of its callback. An `async` callback returns a promise, but `forEach` neither awaits nor collects it — it just fires every callback synchronously and moves on, so code after the loop runs before any async work finishes (and errors become unhandled rejections). **The fix:** use a `for...of` loop with `await` for sequential work, or `Promise.all(arr.map(asyncFn))` for parallel. **Common mistakes:** putting `await` inside a `forEach` callback and expecting the loop to pause, or trying to `await arr.forEach(...)` (it returns `undefined`).

array-forEach-003.explanation: **The problem:** can you stop a `forEach()` early with `break` or `return`? **The answer: no.** `return` inside the callback only exits **that one invocation** (like `continue`), not the loop; `break` is a **SyntaxError** because there's no loop statement to break — the iteration lives inside a function call. **Why:** `forEach` is a method that calls your callback per element; control-flow keywords act on the callback, not the iteration. **The fix:** use `for...of`/`for` (support `break`/`continue`), or `some`/`every` to short-circuit, or `find` to stop at the first match. **Common mistakes:** expecting `return` to end the loop, or `throw`ing just to break out (works but abuses exceptions).

array-includes-001.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, 2, NaN].includes(NaN)` returns `true`, even though `NaN !== NaN`. **Why:** `includes()` compares using the **SameValueZero** algorithm, which treats `NaN` as equal to `NaN` (and `+0` equal to `-0`). So unlike `indexOf` (which uses strict `===` and can't find `NaN`), `includes` *can* detect `NaN`. **Why it matters:** to test for the presence of `NaN`, use `includes`, not `indexOf`. **Common mistakes:** using `indexOf(NaN) !== -1` (always false), or assuming `includes` uses `===` (it uses SameValueZero, the key difference).
array-includes-001.example:
```js
console.log([1, 2, NaN].includes(NaN));   // true  — SameValueZero finds NaN
console.log([1, 2, NaN].indexOf(NaN));    // -1    — === can't match NaN
console.log([0].includes(-0));            // true  — +0 and -0 are equal here
```

array-includes-002.explanation: **The problem:** `['1','2','3'].includes(3)` returns `false`. **Why:** `includes()` does **no type coercion** — it uses SameValueZero, which requires the same type and value. The array holds the **string** `'3'`, and you searched for the **number** `3`; different types, so no match. **Why it matters:** membership checks must use matching types, or you'll miss values. **The fix:** search for `'3'`, or normalize types first (`arr.map(Number).includes(3)`). **Common mistakes:** expecting `==`-style coercion from `includes`/`indexOf` (they're strict), or comparing user input (often strings) against numeric data without converting.
array-includes-002.example:
```js
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].includes(3));   // false — number vs string
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].includes('3')); // true  — matching type
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(Number).includes(3)); // true — normalized
```

array-indexOf-001.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, 2, NaN].indexOf(NaN)` returns `-1` — it can't find `NaN`. **Why:** `indexOf()` compares with **strict equality (`===`)**, and `NaN === NaN` is `false`, so `NaN` is never matched. **Why it matters:** to locate `NaN`, you can't use `indexOf`; use `includes` (SameValueZero) for presence, or `findIndex(Number.isNaN)` for the position. **Common mistakes:** assuming `indexOf` can find `NaN`, or using it for object membership expecting structural equality (it checks reference identity, so it only finds the *same* object).
array-indexOf-001.example:
```js
console.log([1, 2, NaN].indexOf(NaN)); // -1 — === can't match NaN
console.log([1, 2, NaN].includes(NaN)); // true — use includes for presence
console.log([1, 2, NaN].findIndex(Number.isNaN)); // 2 — for the index
```

array-indexOf-002.explanation: **The problem:** `['a','b','a','c'].indexOf('a', 1)` returns `2`, not `0`. **Why:** the second argument is a **start index** — the search begins at index `1`, so the `'a'` at index 0 is skipped, and the next `'a'` (at index 2) is found. **Why it's useful:** you can find subsequent occurrences by passing the previous index + 1, e.g. to collect all matches. **The negative case:** a negative start counts from the end. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the `fromIndex` parameter and expecting `indexOf` to always start at 0, or off-by-one errors when iterating to find all occurrences.

array-join-001.explanation: **The problem:** what separator does `join()` use with no argument? **The answer: a comma `,`** — `['a','b','c'].join()` is `'a,b,c'`. **Why:** the default separator is `,`; pass any string (including `''`) to change it. **A related detail:** `join` coerces elements to strings, and `null`/`undefined`/holes become **empty strings** in the output. **Why it matters:** it's the standard way to build CSV-like strings; `join('')` concatenates with no separator. **Common mistakes:** expecting no separator by default (it's a comma — pass `''` for none), or assuming `null`/`undefined` render as their words (they become empty).
array-join-001.example:
```js
console.log(['a', 'b', 'c'].join());    // 'a,b,c' — default comma
console.log(['a', 'b', 'c'].join(''));  // 'abc'
console.log(['a', 'b', 'c'].join(' - ')); // 'a - b - c'
```

array-join-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, null, undefined, 2].join('-')` returns `'1---2'` (three dashes), not the words `null`/`undefined`. **Why:** `join()` converts elements to strings, but **`null` and `undefined` (and holes) become empty strings**. Four elements always produce **three** separators, so you get `1` + `-` + `''` + `-` + `''` + `-` + `2` = `'1---2'`. **Why it matters:** missing data silently collapses to empty strings while the separators remain, which can corrupt CSV-style output. **Common mistakes:** expecting `'1-null-undefined-2'`, or miscounting the separators — `n` elements give `n - 1` separators regardless of their values.
array-join-002.example:
```js
console.log([1, null, undefined, 2].join('-')); // '1---2' — 4 elems, 3 separators; null/undefined → ''
console.log([1, , 2].join('-'));                // '1--2' — holes too (3 elems, 2 separators)
console.log([1, 2].join('-'));                  // '1-2'
```

array-keys-001.explanation: **The problem:** you want to iterate an array's **indices** lazily. **What `keys()` returns:** an **array iterator** yielding the numeric indices `0, 1, 2, …` (as numbers). **Why useful:** `for (const i of arr.keys())` gives index-only iteration, and unlike `Object.keys` it includes **every** index (holes too) and yields **numbers**, not string keys. **Companions:** `values()` (elements) and `entries()` (`[index, value]`). **Common mistakes:** confusing it with `Object.keys(arr)` (which returns **string** keys and **skips holes**), or expecting `keys()` to return an array (it's an iterator — spread to materialize).
array-keys-001.example:
```js
const a = ['x', 'y', 'z'];
console.log([...a.keys()]); // [0, 1, 2] — numeric indices
for (const i of a.keys()) console.log(i, a[i]); // 0 x | 1 y | 2 z
```

array-keys-002.explanation: **The problem:** `Object.keys` and the array `keys()` iterator disagree on holes and value types. **`Object.keys(['a', , 'c'])` → `['0', '2']`:** it returns **string** keys of *existing* (own enumerable) properties, so it **skips the hole** at index 1. **`[...['a', , 'c'].keys()]` → `[0, 1, 2]`:** the array iterator yields **numeric** indices for **every** position `0..length-1`, including holes. **Why the difference:** `Object.keys` reflects actual properties; the array iterator reflects the index range. **Common mistakes:** assuming both skip holes or both return the same key type — they differ on both counts.
array-keys-002.example:
```js
const sparse = ['a', , 'c']; // hole at index 1
console.log(Object.keys(sparse));    // ['0', '2'] — string keys, hole skipped
console.log([...sparse.keys()]);     // [0, 1, 2]  — numeric, includes the hole
```

array-lastIndexOf-001.explanation: **The problem:** `['a','b','a','c'].lastIndexOf('a')` returns `2`. **Why:** `lastIndexOf()` searches **right-to-left** and returns the index of the **last** matching element — the rightmost `'a'` is at index 2. **The contrast:** `indexOf` returns the **first** match (index 0 here). **Comparison:** like `indexOf`, it uses strict `===`, so it can't find `NaN`. **Why it's useful:** finding the most recent occurrence. **Common mistakes:** expecting it to scan forward, confusing its result with `indexOf`, or assuming it can locate `NaN` (it can't).
array-lastIndexOf-001.example:
```js
const a = ['a', 'b', 'a', 'c'];
console.log(a.lastIndexOf('a')); // 2 — rightmost 'a'
console.log(a.indexOf('a'));     // 0 — leftmost, for contrast
```

array-lastIndexOf-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[NaN].lastIndexOf(NaN)` returns `-1`. **Why:** like `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf()` uses **strict equality (`===`)**, and `NaN === NaN` is `false`, so `NaN` can never be matched — returning `-1` (not found). **Why it matters:** neither `indexOf` nor `lastIndexOf` can locate `NaN`; use `includes` for presence or `findLastIndex(Number.isNaN)` for the last index. **Common mistakes:** assuming `lastIndexOf` behaves like `includes` (SameValueZero) regarding `NaN` — it doesn't; the `indexOf`/`lastIndexOf` pair are the strict-equality outliers.
array-lastIndexOf-002.example:
```js
console.log([NaN].lastIndexOf(NaN));        // -1 — === can't match NaN
console.log([NaN].includes(NaN));           // true — use includes for presence
console.log([1, NaN, NaN].findLastIndex(Number.isNaN)); // 2 — last NaN index
```

array-map-001.explanation: **The problem:** `map()` and `forEach()` look similar but serve different goals. **`map()`:** runs the callback on each element and **returns a new array** of the callback's return values — for **transformation**. **`forEach()`:** runs the callback for **side effects** and returns **`undefined`** — nothing to chain. **Why it matters:** use `map` when you want a transformed array (and you can chain `.filter`/`.reduce`); use `forEach` when you just need to *do* something per element. **Common mistakes:** using `forEach` to build an array via `push` (use `map`), or using `map` purely for side effects and discarding the result (wasteful and misleading).

array-map-002.explanation: **The problem:** `['1','2','3'].map(parseInt)` gives `[1, NaN, NaN]`, not `[1, 2, 3]`. **Why:** `map` calls the callback with **three** arguments — `(value, index, array)` — and `parseInt` takes **two** — `(string, radix)`. So it runs `parseInt('1', 0)`, `parseInt('2', 1)`, `parseInt('3', 2)`. `radix 0` is treated as 10 → `1`; `radix 1` is invalid → `NaN`; `radix 2` (binary) can't parse `'3'` → `NaN`. **The fix:** wrap it — `map(s => parseInt(s, 10))` or `map(Number)`. **Common mistakes:** passing multi-arg built-ins directly to `map` (the index leaks in as an unexpected argument).
array-map-002.example:
```js
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt));           // [1, NaN, NaN] — radix leak
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map((s) => parseInt(s, 10))); // [1, 2, 3]
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(Number));             // [1, 2, 3]
```

array-map-003.explanation: **The problem:** does `map()` change the original array? **The answer: no** — `map()` returns a **new array** and leaves the original intact (it's non-mutating). **The caveat:** if your callback **mutates the element objects** themselves (e.g. `obj.x = 1`), those mutations affect the shared objects because `map` copies **references**, not deep clones. So the array isn't replaced, but the objects inside can be changed. **Why it matters:** treat `map` as pure only if the callback is pure. **Common mistakes:** mutating objects inside a `map` callback and being surprised the originals changed, or assuming `map` deep-copies elements (it doesn't).

array-pop-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `pop()` return on an **empty** array? **The answer: `undefined`** — there's no last element to remove, so it returns `undefined` and the array stays empty (length 0). **Why:** `pop()` removes and returns the final element; with nothing there, it has nothing to give. **Why it matters:** in a `while (arr.length) arr.pop()` drain loop the empty check guards you, but calling `pop()` blindly just yields `undefined` rather than throwing. **Common mistakes:** treating an `undefined` result as "error" vs "empty", or assuming `pop()` throws on an empty array (it doesn't).
array-pop-001.example:
```js
const empty = [];
console.log(empty.pop()); // undefined — nothing to remove
console.log(empty.length); // 0

const a = [1];
console.log(a.pop(), a.pop()); // 1 undefined — second call is empty
```

array-pop-002.explanation: **The problem:** what does `pop()` return, and what's left in the array? **The answer:** it returns the **removed last element** (`3` for `[1,2,3]`) and **mutates** the array to `[1, 2]`. **Why:** `pop()` removes the final element in place, decrements `length`, and hands back that element — not an array. **Why it matters:** `pop` pairs with `push` to use an array as a stack (LIFO). **Common mistakes:** expecting `pop()` to return the remaining array or a single-element array (it returns the value), or forgetting it mutates the original.

array-pop-003.explanation: **The problem:** is `pop()` mutating or does it return a copy? **The answer: it mutates** — `pop()` removes the last element from the **original** array in place and decrements `length`, returning the removed element. **Why:** along with `push`/`shift`/`unshift`/`splice`/`sort`/`reverse`/`fill`/`copyWithin`, it's one of the classic in-place mutators. **Why it matters:** in immutable/state code (e.g. React), mutating with `pop` can cause stale renders — copy first (`arr.slice(0, -1)`) instead. **Common mistakes:** assuming `pop()` returns a new array, or using it on shared/state arrays without copying.

array-push-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `push()` return — the array or something else? **The answer: the new `length`** of the array after the elements are appended. **Why:** returning the length lets you cheaply track size or use it in loops; `push` mutates the array in place and hands back a number, not the array. **Why it matters:** you can't chain off `push` as if it returned the array (`arr.push(x).push(y)` fails — the second `push` runs on a number). **Common mistakes:** expecting `push` to return the array (it returns the count) or the pushed element.

array-push-002.explanation: **The problem:** append **all** elements of array `b` onto `a` in one call, without creating a new array. **The answer: `a.push(...b)`** — spread expands `b` into individual arguments, so each element is pushed onto `a` in place. **Why not `a.push(b)`:** that appends `b` as a **single nested array** element. **Why not `a.concat(b)`:** it returns a **new** array and doesn't mutate `a`. **Why not `a.append`:** there's no such method. **The caveat:** for very large `b`, spread can hit the argument-count limit — use a loop or `for...of` then. **Common mistakes:** pushing the whole array, or expecting `concat` to mutate.

array-push-003.explanation: **The problem:** does `push()` mutate or return a new array? **The answer: it mutates** — `push()` appends to the **end** of the original array in place and returns the new **length** (a number, not the array). **Why:** it's an in-place mutator, like `pop`/`shift`/`unshift`/`splice`. **Why it matters:** in immutable contexts (React state), prefer non-mutating appends like `[...arr, x]` or `arr.concat(x)` so references change and renders trigger. **Common mistakes:** assuming `push` returns the array (it returns the length), or mutating shared/state arrays directly.

array-reduce-001.explanation: **The problem:** `reduce()` on an **empty** array with **no `initialValue`** throws a `TypeError`. **Why:** without an initial value, `reduce` uses the **first element** as the starting accumulator — but an empty array has no first element, so there's nothing to start from, and the spec mandates a `TypeError` rather than guessing. **The fix:** always pass an `initialValue` (e.g. `0`, `[]`, `{}`); then an empty array simply returns that initial value. **Why it matters:** reducing data of unknown length is unsafe without an initial value. **Common mistakes:** omitting `initialValue` and crashing on empty inputs, or assuming it returns `undefined` for empty arrays (it throws).

array-reduce-002.explanation: **The problem:** how many times does the callback run for `[10].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n)` (no `initialValue`)? **The answer: `0`.** **Why:** with no `initialValue`, `reduce` takes the **single element** (`10`) as the accumulator and **skips** calling the callback for it — there's no second element to combine with, so the callback never fires; `reduce` returns `10` directly. **Why it matters:** for a one-element array without an initial value, the callback (and its side effects) won't run. **Common mistakes:** expecting one invocation, or a `TypeError` (that's only for an *empty* array with no initial value).

array-reduce-003.explanation: **The problem:** `initialValue` changes **where** iteration starts. **With `initialValue`:** the accumulator begins as `initialValue` and the callback runs starting at **index 0** (every element is processed). **Without `initialValue`:** the accumulator begins as the **element at index 0**, and the callback runs starting at **index 1** (index 0 is consumed as the seed, not visited by the callback). **Why it matters:** the count of callback invocations and the handling of the first element differ, which affects accumulators like objects/strings. **Common mistakes:** forgetting that without an initial value the first element bypasses the callback, or that an empty array without an initial value throws.

array-reduceRight-001.explanation: **The problem:** `reduce()` and `reduceRight()` differ only in **direction**. **`reduce()`** folds **left-to-right** (index 0 → end); **`reduceRight()`** folds **right-to-left** (last index → 0). Everything else — `initialValue` rules, callback signature `(acc, cur, i, arr)`, empty-array behavior — is identical. **Why it matters:** direction changes the result for non-commutative operations like string building, subtraction, or array concatenation. **When to use `reduceRight`:** right-associative composition or processing from the end. **Common mistakes:** assuming the direction doesn't matter (it does for order-dependent folds), or that `reduceRight` reverses the array (it only changes traversal order).
array-reduceRight-001.example:
```js
const chars = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
console.log(chars.reduce((acc, c) => acc + c, ''));      // 'abc' — left to right
console.log(chars.reduceRight((acc, c) => acc + c, '')); // 'cba' — right to left
```

array-reduceRight-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[['a','b'],['c','d'],['e','f']].reduceRight((acc, cur) => acc.concat(cur), [])` yields `['e','f','c','d','a','b']`. **Why:** `reduceRight` processes elements **right-to-left**, so the **last** sub-array `['e','f']` is concatenated first, then `['c','d']`, then `['a','b']` — building `['e','f','c','d','a','b']`. **Why not `['a','b','c','d','e','f']`:** that's what `reduce` (left-to-right) would produce. **Why not a full reverse:** within each pair, order is preserved (`'e','f'` stays `'e','f'`); only the **groups** are reversed. **Common mistakes:** expecting a deep reverse, or confusing the group order with element order.

array-reverse-001.explanation: **The problem:** does `reverse()` return a new array or change the original? **The answer: it mutates** — `reverse()` reverses the array's elements **in place** and returns a **reference to the same** (now reversed) array. **Why it matters:** `const b = a.reverse()` makes `b` and `a` the **same** reversed array, not a copy — a common source of accidental shared mutation. **The non-mutating option:** `toReversed()` (ES2023) or `[...a].reverse()`. **Common mistakes:** assuming `reverse()` leaves the original intact, or that the returned value is an independent copy.

array-reverse-002.explanation: **The problem:** you want to reverse **without mutating** the original. **The answer: `toReversed()`** (ES2023) — it returns a **new** reversed array and leaves the source untouched. **Why it exists:** the classic `reverse()` mutates in place, which is dangerous for shared/state arrays; `toReversed` is the immutable counterpart (joining `toSorted`, `toSpliced`, and `with`). **Why the other names are wrong:** `reverseClone`, `reverseCopy`, `immutableReverse` aren't real methods. **The pre-ES2023 idiom:** `[...arr].reverse()`. **Common mistakes:** reaching for a made-up method name, or using `reverse()` on state and causing stale renders.

array-shift-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `shift()` do and return? **The answer:** it **removes the first element**, returns it, and **mutates** the array (every remaining element shifts down one index, length decreases). **Why it matters:** `shift`/`push` together make a queue (FIFO); but `shift` is **O(n)** because all elements re-index, unlike `pop` which is O(1). **The empty case:** `shift()` on `[]` returns `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** assuming it returns the remaining array (it returns the removed element), forgetting the performance cost on large arrays, or using it on shared/state arrays without copying.
array-shift-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3];
const first = a.shift();
console.log(first); // 1     — removed element
console.log(a);     // [2, 3] — mutated, indices shifted
console.log([].shift()); // undefined — empty array
```

array-shift-002.explanation: **The problem:** what does `const v = a.shift()` produce for `a = [1, 2, 3]`? **The answer:** `v` is `1` (the removed first element) and `a` becomes `[2, 3]` (mutated). **Why:** `shift()` removes and returns the **first** element, then re-indexes the rest down by one. **Why not `undefined`/`[1, 2, 3]`:** the array isn't empty and `shift` does mutate it. **Why not `[1]`:** it returns the **value**, not a single-element array. **Common mistakes:** confusing `shift` (front) with `pop` (back), or expecting the original array to be unchanged.

array-slice-001.explanation: **The problem:** does `slice()` modify the original array? **The answer: no** — `slice(start, end)` returns a **shallow copy** of the `[start, end)` portion and leaves the original untouched. **Why it's useful:** quick copies (`arr.slice()` clones the whole array), safe sub-ranges, and non-mutating alternatives to `splice`. **The shallow caveat:** nested objects are shared by reference between the source and the slice. **Don't confuse it with `splice`,** which **mutates** and removes/inserts. **Common mistakes:** mixing up `slice` (copy, non-mutating) and `splice` (mutating), or expecting a deep copy.
array-slice-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const part = a.slice(1, 3);
console.log(part); // [2, 3] — copy of [start, end)
console.log(a);    // [1, 2, 3, 4] — unchanged
console.log(a.slice() === a); // false — slice() clones
```

array-slice-002.explanation: **The problem:** `['a','b','c','d','e'].slice(1, -1)` returns `['b','c','d']`. **Why:** `start` is inclusive and `end` is exclusive; a **negative `end`** counts from the end, so `-1` means "up to (but not including) the last element" — index `length - 1` = 4. So it copies indices 1, 2, 3 → `['b','c','d']`. **Why it's handy:** `slice(1, -1)` trims the first and last elements in one call. **Common mistakes:** treating `end` as inclusive, or thinking `-1` selects the last element (it's the exclusive bound — the last element is dropped).
array-slice-002.example:
```js
const a = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'];
console.log(a.slice(1, -1)); // ['b', 'c', 'd'] — drop first and last
console.log(a.slice(-2));    // ['d', 'e'] — last two
console.log(a.slice(2));     // ['c', 'd', 'e'] — from index 2 to end
```

array-some-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `some()` return for an **empty** array? **The answer: `false`** — vacuously, since there's no element that passes the test. **Why:** `some()` returns `true` only if it finds at least one element for which the callback is truthy; with zero elements, it never finds one. This is the mirror of `every([])` being `true`. **Why it matters:** `items.some(isInvalid)` is `false` for empty inputs (nothing invalid) — sometimes intended, sometimes a bug. **Common mistakes:** expecting `true` for `[]`, or forgetting the symmetric quirk with `every`.
array-some-001.example:
```js
console.log([].some((x) => x > 0));        // false — vacuously false
console.log([1, 2, 3].some((x) => x > 2)); // true  — 3 passes
console.log([1, 2].some((x) => x > 5));    // false — none pass
console.log([].every((x) => x > 0));       // true  — the symmetric case
```

array-some-002.explanation: **The problem:** how does `some()` short-circuit? **The answer:** it stops iterating **the moment the callback returns truthy** and returns `true`, skipping all remaining elements. If none pass, it visits everything and returns `false`. **Why:** once one element satisfies "at least one", the answer is decided, so further work is wasted. **Why it matters:** side effects after the first match won't run, and it's efficient on large arrays. **Common mistakes:** confusing it with `every` (which short-circuits on the first **falsy**), or assuming `some` always visits every element (it stops at the first truthy).

array-some-003.explanation: **The problem:** does `some()` run the callback for empty slots (holes)? **The answer: no** — like `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, and `every`, `some()` **skips holes** in sparse arrays; the callback is never invoked for an empty slot. **Why it matters:** a hole can't make `some` return `true` since the predicate never runs on it. **The contrast:** the `find`/`findIndex`/`findLast` family and the `entries`/`keys`/`values` iterators **do** visit holes (as `undefined`). **Common mistakes:** assuming all iteration methods treat holes the same — they split into hole-skipping (`some` and friends) and hole-visiting (`find` family, iterators).

array-sort-001.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, 30, 4, 21, 100000].sort()` gives `[1, 100000, 21, 30, 4]`, not numeric order. **Why:** the default `sort()` converts elements to **strings** and compares them **lexicographically** (by UTF-16 code units). As strings, `'100000' < '21' < '30' < '4'` because `'1' < '2' < '3' < '4'` at the first character. **The fix:** pass a comparator — `sort((a, b) => a - b)` for ascending numbers. **Why it's a classic trap:** numbers sort "alphabetically" by default. **Common mistakes:** sorting numbers without a comparator, or assuming `sort()` is numeric for number arrays.

array-sort-002.explanation: **The problem:** does `sort()` return a new array or mutate? **The answer: it mutates** — `sort()` orders the array **in place** and returns a **reference to the same** array. **Why it matters:** `const b = a.sort()` makes `b` and `a` the same sorted array; mutating shared/state arrays this way causes subtle bugs (and stale renders in React). **The immutable option:** `toSorted()` (ES2023) or `[...a].sort()`. **Also note:** `sort` is stable (equal elements keep their relative order) in modern engines. **Common mistakes:** assuming `sort()` leaves the original untouched, or that the return value is a copy.

array-sort-003.explanation: **The problem:** where do `undefined` values and empty slots (holes) land after a default `sort()`? **The answer:** all **`undefined` values sort to the end**, and **empty slots come after even the `undefined`s** — at the very end of the array. **Why:** `sort` moves `undefined`s to the end **without** calling the comparator on them, and holes are pushed past everything (they're not real elements). **Why it matters:** sparse or `undefined`-containing arrays don't sort the way you'd expect, and your comparator never sees those values. **Common mistakes:** writing a comparator assuming it handles `undefined`/holes (it's never called for them), or expecting them at the start.
array-sort-003.example:
```js
const a = [3, undefined, 1, , 2]; // value undefined at idx 1, hole at idx 3
a.sort((x, y) => x - y);
console.log(a);        // [1, 2, 3, undefined, <1 empty item>]
console.log(a.length); // 5 — undefined precedes the hole at the very end
```

array-splice-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `splice()` **return** (versus what it does to the array)? **The answer:** it returns an **array of the removed elements** — or an **empty array `[]`** if nothing was removed (e.g. a pure insertion). Separately, it **mutates** the original array in place. **Why two effects:** `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` can delete and/or insert; the return value reports only what was deleted. **Why it matters:** to get the modified array, read the original (it's mutated); the return value is the removed slice. **Common mistakes:** expecting `splice` to return the modified array (that's the mutated original), or assuming it's non-mutating like `slice`.
array-splice-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const removed = a.splice(1, 2); // remove 2 elements from index 1
console.log(removed); // [2, 3] — the removed elements
console.log(a);       // [1, 4]  — mutated original
console.log([1, 2].splice(0, 0, 'x')); // [] — pure insert removes nothing
```

array-splice-002.explanation: **The problem:** what does `[1,2,3,4,5].splice(2, 0, 'a', 'b')` do? **The answer:** it **inserts** `'a'` and `'b'` at index 2 **without removing** anything — `deleteCount` is `0`. The array becomes `[1, 2, 'a', 'b', 3, 4, 5]`, and `splice` returns `[]` (nothing removed). **Why:** the signature is `splice(start, deleteCount, ...itemsToInsert)`; a `deleteCount` of `0` means "insert here". **Why it matters:** this is the idiom for inserting at a position in place. **Common mistakes:** thinking it replaces elements at index 2 (that needs `deleteCount > 0`), or that `start` is `'a'` (the first arg is always the index).
array-splice-002.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const removed = a.splice(2, 0, 'a', 'b'); // insert at index 2, delete none
console.log(a);       // [1, 2, 'a', 'b', 3, 4, 5]
console.log(removed); // [] — nothing removed
```

array-splice-003.explanation: **The problem:** `splice()` and `slice()` are easy to confuse. **`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)`:** **mutates** the array (removes and/or inserts) and **returns the removed elements**. **`slice(start, end)`:** **does not mutate** — it returns a **shallow copy** of the `[start, end)` range. **The mnemonic:** *spl*ice changes the array (it has an extra letter and extra power); slice just copies. **Why it matters:** using `splice` where you meant `slice` corrupts the source array. **Common mistakes:** swapping them, or assuming both take the same arguments (`slice`'s second arg is an end index; `splice`'s is a delete count).
array-splice-003.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(a.slice(1, 3)); // [2, 3] — copy, non-mutating
console.log(a);             // [1, 2, 3, 4] — unchanged

const b = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(b.splice(1, 2)); // [2, 3] — removed elements
console.log(b);              // [1, 4]  — mutated
```

array-toReversed-001.explanation: **The problem:** `reverse()` and `toReversed()` both reverse — the key difference is mutation. **`reverse()`:** reverses **in place** and returns the **same** (mutated) array. **`toReversed()` (ES2023):** returns a **new** reversed array and leaves the original **unchanged**. **Why it matters:** `toReversed` is safe for shared/state arrays where you must not mutate (React state, props); `reverse` risks surprising side effects. **The pre-ES2023 equivalent:** `[...arr].reverse()`. **Common mistakes:** using `reverse()` on data you didn't mean to change, or assuming `toReversed` mutates like its older sibling.

array-toReversed-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, , 3].toReversed()` returns `[3, undefined, 1]` — the hole becomes `undefined`. **Why:** the ES2023 immutable methods (`toReversed`, `toSorted`, `toSpliced`, `with`) operate as if reading every index `0..length-1`, so **holes are read as `undefined`** and the result is a **dense** array. Reversing `[1, hole, 3]` gives `[3, undefined, 1]`. **The contrast:** the mutating `reverse()` preserves holes. **Why it matters:** these newer methods normalize sparseness to `undefined`. **Common mistakes:** expecting the hole to stay a hole (`[3, , 1]`), or that `toReversed` drops it.
array-toReversed-002.example:
```js
const a = [1, , 3]; // hole at index 1
console.log(a.toReversed()); // [3, undefined, 1] — dense, hole → undefined
const b = [1, , 3];
b.reverse();
console.log(1 in b); // false — mutating reverse keeps the hole
```

array-toSorted-001.explanation: **The problem:** `toSorted()` vs `sort()` — same ordering, different mutation. **`sort()`:** sorts **in place** and returns the same mutated array. **`toSorted()` (ES2023):** returns a **new** sorted array and leaves the original **unchanged**. Both accept the same optional comparator and default to **string** comparison without one. **Why it matters:** `toSorted` is the immutable choice for state/shared arrays; no need for `[...arr].sort()`. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the comparator for numbers with **either** method (both string-sort by default), or assuming `toSorted` mutates.

array-toSorted-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1, 10, 21, 2].toSorted()` returns `[1, 10, 2, 21]`, not numeric order. **Why:** like `sort()`, `toSorted()` **with no comparator** converts elements to **strings** and sorts lexicographically — `'1' < '10' < '2' < '21'` because `'1' < '2'` at the first character and `'10' < '2'`. **The fix:** pass a comparator — `toSorted((a, b) => a - b)`. **Why it's a trap:** `toSorted` being newer/immutable doesn't change the default string comparison. **Common mistakes:** assuming `toSorted` is numeric by default, or that only `sort` has the string-sort quirk.
array-toSorted-002.example:
```js
console.log([1, 10, 21, 2].toSorted());            // [1, 10, 2, 21] — string order
console.log([1, 10, 21, 2].toSorted((a, b) => a - b)); // [1, 2, 10, 21]
```

array-toSpliced-001.explanation: **The problem:** you want `splice`'s remove/insert power **without** mutating the original. **`toSpliced(start, deleteCount, ...items)` (ES2023):** returns a **new** array with the changes applied and leaves the source **unchanged**. **The key difference from `splice`:** `splice` mutates and returns the **removed** elements; `toSpliced` doesn't mutate and returns the **resulting** array. **Why it matters:** ideal for updating state arrays immutably in one call. **Common mistakes:** expecting `toSpliced` to return the removed elements (that's `splice`), or assuming it mutates like `splice`.
array-toSpliced-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 5];
const b = a.toSpliced(2, 0, 3, 4); // insert 3,4 at index 2
console.log(b); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] — new array
console.log(a); // [1, 2, 5]       — original untouched
```

array-toSpliced-002.explanation: **The problem:** `const b = a.toSpliced(1, 0, 'Feb')` for `a = ['Jan','Mar','Apr']` — what are `a` and `b`? **The answer:** `a` stays `['Jan','Mar','Apr']` (unchanged) and `b` is `['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr']` (the new array with `'Feb'` inserted at index 1, deleting none). **Why:** `toSpliced` is the **non-mutating** sibling of `splice` — it builds and returns a new array, never touching the source. **Why it matters:** this is the clean way to insert into a state array without copying first. **Common mistakes:** expecting `a` to also change (it won't), or that `b` is the removed elements (it's the full result).

array-unshift-001.explanation: **The problem:** what does `unshift()` return? **The answer: the new `length`** of the array after the elements are prepended (mirroring `push`). **Why:** `unshift` adds elements to the **front** in place and hands back the count, not the array. **The performance note:** like `shift`, it's **O(n)** because every existing element re-indexes. **Why it matters:** you can't chain off `unshift` as if it returned the array. **Common mistakes:** expecting it to return the array or the added elements, or ignoring the re-indexing cost on large arrays.

array-unshift-002.explanation: **The problem:** one `unshift(1, 2, 3)` vs three separate `unshift(1)`, `unshift(2)`, `unshift(3)` give different orders. **Why:** `unshift(1, 2, 3)` inserts all three **at once**, preserving their order at the front → `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. But calling `unshift` **three times** prepends one element each call: after `unshift(1)` → `[1,4,5]`, then `unshift(2)` → `[2,1,4,5]`, then `unshift(3)` → `[3,2,1,4,5]`. Each new element jumps ahead of the previously prepended ones, **reversing** them. **Common mistakes:** assuming repeated single `unshift`s build the same order as one multi-arg call (they reverse).

array-values-001.explanation: **The problem:** how do you iterate an array's **values** via an explicit iterator? **What `values()` returns:** an **array iterator** that yields each **element value** in order. **Why it exists:** it's the counterpart to `keys()` (indices) and `entries()` (`[index, value]`), and it's exactly what `for...of` uses under the hood (`arr[Symbol.iterator] === arr.values`). **A detail:** the iterator is **stateful and one-shot** — once consumed, it's exhausted. **Common mistakes:** expecting `values()` to return an array (it's an iterator — spread with `[...arr.values()]`), or reusing an exhausted iterator (see the next card).
array-values-001.example:
```js
const a = ['x', 'y', 'z'];
const it = a.values();
console.log(it.next().value); // 'x'
console.log([...a.values()]); // ['x', 'y', 'z'] — materialize
for (const v of a.values()) console.log(v); // x | y | z
```

array-values-002.explanation: **The problem:** after fully consuming an iterator in one `for...of`, a second loop over the **same** iterator logs **nothing**. **Why:** an iterator is **stateful and single-use** — once it reaches `done: true`, it stays exhausted; it doesn't reset. The first loop drains it, so the second has nothing left. **The fix:** call `arr.values()` again to get a **fresh** iterator, or loop over the array directly (each `for...of` on the array creates a new iterator). **Why it matters:** storing an iterator and iterating it twice is a common bug. **Common mistakes:** expecting iterators to be reusable like arrays, or that a new `for...of` rewinds an existing iterator.

array-with-001.explanation: **The problem:** you want to change one element **without mutating** the array. **`with(index, value)` (ES2023):** returns a **new** array identical to the original except that `index` holds `value`; the original is **unchanged**. It's the immutable replacement for `arr[i] = value`. **Why it matters:** updating a single item in a state array becomes a one-liner with no copy step (`arr.with(i, v)` instead of `arr.map((x, j) => j === i ? v : x)`). **It supports negative indices** (counting from the end). **Common mistakes:** expecting `with` to mutate (it returns a copy), or using bracket assignment on state arrays (mutates).
array-with-001.example:
```js
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const b = a.with(2, 99);
console.log(b); // [1, 2, 99, 4, 5] — new array
console.log(a); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  — original untouched
console.log(a.with(-1, 0)); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 0] — negative index
```

array-with-002.explanation: **The problem:** `[1,2,3].with(10, 99)` throws a **`RangeError`**. **Why:** `with(index, value)` requires the index to be **within bounds** (`0 <= index < length`, or a valid negative offset). Index `10` is past the end of a 3-element array, so it throws rather than extending or padding the array. **The contrast:** bracket assignment `a[10] = 99` would silently grow the array and create holes — `with` is stricter. **Why it matters:** `with` won't accidentally create sparse arrays. **Common mistakes:** expecting `with` to append at an out-of-range index (use `push`/spread for that), or that it returns the array unchanged on a bad index (it throws).
